# How these workflows fail, and how to catch it {#sec-failure-modes}

A skeptical Biometrics head's first question about any AI-assisted
workflow is "show me how this fails and how I would catch it." The
applied examples answer that question inside their own lifecycle
stages. This appendix consolidates the four failure patterns that cut
across examples: prompt injection through artifact content,
confabulated evidence citations, benchmark gaming with silent coverage
gaps, and version skew between artifacts the agent silently combines.
For each pattern the appendix names the failure, the control in this
book designed to catch it, and what remains unevidenced.

This appendix proposes no workflow, so it runs no lifecycle stages and
declares no maturity level. It is a cross-cutting reader's guide to
controls defined in @sec-workflow-rounding-skill and
@sec-workflow-sap-change, collected in one place.

## Prompt injection through artifact content

The failure: the agent reads untrusted text as instructions. A draft
SAP paragraph, a code comment, or a review note can carry phrasing
that steers the agent --- to prefer one SAP version, to skip an
awkward check, or to interpret an ambiguous requirement instead of
escalating it. The agent treats content as context, and content can
push.

The control is to make the task contract uninterpretable in the
relevant directions. In @sec-workflow-sap-change, conflicting
duplicate SAP declarations escalate instead of silently using the
first, and an SAP excerpt without window parameters refuses selection
with an ESCALATE message rather than an invented window. The contract
fixes the identifier chain every finding must cite
(SAP Section 8.2 -> AWLO/AWHI/AWTARGET -> ANL01FL -> Table 14-3.01
rows), so there is no offered path by which artifact wording alone can
authorize a different selection.

TODO: no live injection probe has been run against these workflows, so
the control above is a design claim, not red-team evidence. A first
probe would plant a steering sentence in a draft SAP excerpt and check
that the run escalates rather than complies.

## Confabulated evidence citations

The failure: a finding cites artifacts that do not say what is
claimed. A file and line number look verifiable, but the cited lines
may be a wrapper, a comment, or an unrelated helper rather than the
formatting call the finding describes. Precision of citation is not
accuracy of citation.

The control is to check the cited content, not the citation format.
@sec-workflow-rounding-skill records this lesson in its probe results:
the catalog preserves excluded candidates, for example `R/fmt.R:37`,
which pads text formatted at line 33 and does not round numeric input.
That correction shows why scanner hits are coverage evidence, not
automatic findings. Every finding in @sec-workflow-sap-change must cite its
full evidence chain back to a pinned artifact, and the "Try it
yourself" exercise trains the reviewer to verify each link rather than
accept the chain on presentation.

TODO: the book has no measured rate of confabulated citations from a
held-out benchmark, so reviewers should assume the failure recurs and
budget check time accordingly until such a measurement exists.

## Benchmark gaming and silent coverage gaps

The failure: the agent reports "checked" without a minimum check
list, or a benchmark passes because the hard cases were never
selected. A green report then certifies work that never happened. This
is the quietest failure in this appendix, because nothing looks wrong.

The control is a required coverage statement on every run, including
rules left unchecked. @sec-workflow-rounding-skill requires coverage
and unchecked rules in the minimum report. The maxim behind the
requirement comes from the motivating chapter
(@sec-workflow-rounding-prompt): an ad hoc response can state which
files and rules it checked, but with no required file list, silence is
not evidence that every file or rule was reviewed.
@sec-workflow-sap-change reports coverage as "6 of
6 defined cases with 0 skipped and 0 failed" and re-checks all six
cases on every re-run, with cost and latency labelled as unmeasured
rather than silently omitted.

TODO: the six SAP cases and the rounding benchmark rows are
author-defined; an independent check that the minimum check lists are
complete (rather than merely fully executed) has not been done.

## Version skew between combined artifacts

The failure: the agent silently combines inputs from different
versions --- a selection derived under SAP v1.0 presented as
satisfying a v1.1 claim, results computed by one code version
described by another's documentation, or a library whose behavior
changed under a floating reference.

The control is to pin every input and refuse mismatched stamps.
@sec-workflow-sap-change rejects a v1.0-stamped selection presented
for a v1.1 claim without interpretation, and its release record pins
the tested combination (code version, SAP excerpt versions, extracts
by sha256, R version, benchmark result). The rounding chapters pin
their external reference to a commit SHA
rather than a branch, following the deploy rule: install an immutable
version that matches the accepted benchmark, and do not test one
commit while deploying a moving `main` branch. A reader applying the
same discipline pins the model or agent version behind a benchmark
before comparing runs.

TODO: the manuscript pins code, data extracts, and one library
reference; it does not yet pin the agent or model versions used in
each benchmark run, so cross-run comparisons carry that caveat.

## Summary

Each failure pattern above pairs a concrete way the work can go wrong
with a control already present in the applied examples: escalation
conditions against injection, content-level citation review against
confabulation, required coverage statements against silent gaps, and
version-stamp refusal against skew. The TODO markers record where the
catch is a designed control rather than a measured one. Closing those
markers --- one planted probe, one citation error rate, one
completeness review, one version-pinning pass --- is the proposed
adversarial test program for the next planning cycle.
